subfield: Condensed matter physics / photovoltaic semiconductor physics
motivation: Miyasaka first used metal-halide perovskites as photovoltaic absorbers in 2009. In 2012 Park made the first stable solid-state perovskite cell, and Snaith showed that perovskites carry charge themselves over long distances, so a mesoporous scaffold was not needed. Together their work founded a new class of semiconductors. These solution-processed, defect-tolerant materials combine sharp absorption edges, long carrier diffusion lengths and low non-radiative losses. Physicists did not expect this in polycrystalline films made at low temperature. Within about a decade, single-junction cells went from 4% to above 26% efficiency, and perovskite–silicon tandems now exceed 33%. This work has changed our understanding of defects, mixed ionic–electronic conduction and photon recycling in semiconductors. It also offers a credible route to cheaper, higher-efficiency photovoltaics on the terawatt scale needed for climate mitigation.
